title: Tree Climbing Gear Checklist: Starter to Pro Kit
h1: Tree Climbing Gear: The Complete Checklist
meta: A tree climbing gear checklist from first kit to pro setup: saddle, rope, hitch or device, lanyard, carabiners, helmet, throw line, spurs and a hand saw.
dek: Everything a working climber carries, why each piece matters, and where it makes sense to spend more.

sections.h: Start with training, then buy the tree climbing gear
p: Tree climbing gear is life-support equipment. Before you spend money on a kit, get trained by a qualified arborist climber or a recognized training program, and learn the gear in a controlled setting low to the ground. Every item on this list should meet the applicable ANSI Z133 requirements and be used according to its manufacturer's instructions.

This checklist walks through a full kit in the order you will use it on a typical climb: get a line in the tree, tie in, ascend, position, work and come down. For each item we cover what it does, what to look for, and where a beginner can save money versus where a working climber should spend it.

A rule that holds across the whole kit: buy compatible pieces. Your rope, hitch cord or device, carabiners and saddle bridge all work together, and a mismatch in diameter or gate type causes more problems than any single cheap item.

sections.h: Saddle: the piece you will feel all day
p: Your saddle is where you spend your working hours, so comfort and adjustability matter more here than almost anywhere else. Arborist saddles have a wide waist belt, leg loops, side D-rings for lanyard attachment and a bridge or attachment point for your climbing system. Many also have rails or loops for hanging tools and gear.

European-style saddles with a sliding bridge, like the Petzl Sequoia or TreeMotion, give a lot of freedom of movement and suit both moving rope and stationary rope climbing. Simpler saddles cost less and work fine for climbers who mostly do removals. Try a saddle on and hang in it if you can, and look at our saddles and harnesses for the range of styles.

Inspect webbing, stitching, bridge and buckles before every climb, and retire the bridge on the schedule the manufacturer gives. A chest harness is optional but helps some climbers stay upright and can carry a device in some SRS setups.

sections.h: Climbing rope and the system that grips it
p: Your climbing line needs to meet the strength requirements of ANSI Z133 and be approved for climbing by its manufacturer. Most climbers start with a 1/2-inch or 11.5 to 13 mm line. A 16-strand rope with a firm cover is forgiving with friction hitches, while 24-strand and kernmantle static ropes tend to run better in mechanical devices. Our climbing rope section breaks these down.

On a moving rope system you need a friction hitch on a hitch cord, a micro pulley to tend it, and a way to attach to the bridge. Later, many climbers add a mechanical friction device such as a ZigZag, Rope Runner Pro or SpiderJack. These devices are popular, but they are not plug-and-play: each is designed for a specific range of rope diameters and constructions, so check the instructions before matching one to your line.
A 150-foot line covers most residential trees in a doubled-rope system. Plan on a second line eventually, since rope lasts longer when you can rest one and inspect it properly.

A positioning lanyard is your second point of attachment when you are cutting. Most climbers use an adjustable rope lanyard with a mechanical adjuster or a hitch, and many removal climbers also carry a wire-core flipline for working near a running saw. Choose a length that lets you wrap the trunks you usually climb, with room to spare.

Life-support carabiners must be self-closing and self-locking; check the current Z133 for the gate requirements, and note that most arborists use triple-action auto-locking gates. Aluminum is light and plenty strong for most connections; steel is heavier but resists wear where rope runs over the carabiner. Keep a few non-locking accessory carabiners for hanging tools, never for life support.
list: Adjustable rope lanyard with adjuster or hitch
Wire-core flipline for removal work
Auto-locking carabiners (most climbers use triple-action) for every life-support connection
Accessory carabiners for saws, rope bags and tools only

p: A climbing-style helmet with a chin strap stays on your head if you swing into a stem or take a fall. Look for a helmet rated for the work you do, with slots for a visor and hearing protection. Popular arborist helmets include the Petzl Vertex, Kask Super Plasma and Pfanner Protos, all in our helmets section.
Add safety glasses or a mesh visor, and earmuffs or plugs for saw work. Replace a helmet after a significant impact, and follow the maker's service-life guidance.

sections.h: Throw line, throw weight and line storage
p: The easiest way to set a high tie-in point from the ground is with a throw weight and thin throw line. A starter kit is a couple of 10 to 14 oz throw weights, 150 to 180 feet of line and a cube or bag to store it so it pays out without tangles.

Practice in an open yard before you need it on a job. Larger throwing tools like a big-shot launcher help on tall trees, but always keep people clear of the landing zone. Take a look at the throw weights and line we list.

Climbing spurs, also called gaffs or climbers, are for removals and emergency access only. Spurring a tree you are pruning wounds living tissue with every step and is not acceptable practice. If you mostly prune, you may never need them.

If you do removal work, look at shank length, pad comfort, strap style and gaff length. Aluminum spurs save weight on long days, and steel spurs are durable and cost less. Keep gaffs sharp to the manufacturer's profile, and get trained on spur climbing before you trust them at height.

sections.h: Hand saw and the rest of the working kit
p: A sharp pruning saw on a lanyard handles most of the cutting a pruning climber does. A curved saw around 13 inches, like a Silky Zubat, is a common first choice, with a scabbard that clips to your saddle. Add a hand pruner for small cuts and clean finish work.
Round out the kit with a rope bag, a first-aid kit on the truck, gloves and boots with good ankle support. Starter climbers can get to work with the items below and add more as their work demands it.
list: Saddle with bridge and gear loops
Climbing line approved for climbing, plus a hitch cord and micro pulley or a compatible device
Adjustable positioning lanyard
Auto-locking carabiners for life-support connections
Helmet with chin strap, eye and hearing protection
Throw weights, throw line and storage
Pruning saw with scabbard and lanyard
Spurs, only if you do removals

faq.q: What tree climbing gear does a beginner need first?
faq.a: A saddle, a climbing rope approved for climbing, a friction hitch cord with a micro pulley or a compatible device, a positioning lanyard, auto-locking carabiners, a helmet, and a throw line kit. Get trained before you climb.

faq.q: How much does a starter tree climbing kit cost?
faq.a: A basic kit runs from several hundred dollars to over a thousand depending on the saddle and whether you add a mechanical device. The saddle and rope are usually the largest costs.

faq.q: Do I need spurs to climb trees?
faq.a: No. Spurs are for removals and emergency access only. Pruning climbers should never use spurs on trees they intend to keep.

faq.q: How often should I inspect my climbing gear?
faq.a: Before every climb, plus a more thorough periodic inspection as the manufacturer recommends. Retire anything that is cut, glazed, cracked or has been shock-loaded.

title: Husqvarna 372XP vs 572XP: Which 70cc Saw to Buy
meta: Husqvarna 372XP vs 572XP compared for tree work: power, AutoTune vs carburetor, weight, maintenance and which 70cc saw fits a removal crew best.
dek: Two 70cc Husqvarna workhorses, one classic and one modern, compared the way a removal crew would use them.

p: The Husqvarna 372XP vs 572XP question comes up on almost every removal crew. Both are 70cc-class professional saws meant for felling, bucking and big limb work, and both run bars in the 18 to 28 inch range for most tree work. The difference is age and technology: the 372XP is a classic design with a conventional carburetor that crews have run for decades, while the 572XP is Husqvarna's newer saw in the same size class with AutoTune electronic fuel management.

If you want the short answer: the 572XP is the more modern and slightly more powerful saw, with AutoTune that adjusts the fuel mixture as conditions change. The 372XP is simpler, easy to work on and loved by people who know how to tune a carburetor. Availability of the 372XP varies by market, since emissions rules have pushed it out in some places.
The rest of this guide covers what that means on a real job, and how to pick. For model details, see our Husqvarna 372XP and Husqvarna 572XP pages.

Both saws sit at about 70cc. Husqvarna rates the 572XP at a bit more power than the 372XP, and on the job it feels a little stronger in big wood, especially with a longer bar buried in a cut. The 372XP has a reputation for snappy throttle response and plenty of torque for its size, which is part of why it has such a following.

In practice, a sharp chain and a well-matched bar make more difference to cutting speed than the gap between these two saws. Either one will handle typical removals, storm cleanup and firewood-sized bucking. The 572XP pulls ahead when you run longer bars or cut dense hardwood all day.

If you are coming from a 50cc or 60cc saw, either one will feel like a big step up in how fast it pulls through a 20-inch log. If you already run a 90cc saw for the big stuff, a 70cc saw becomes the everyday removal saw that you reach for first because it is lighter to carry around the yard and easier to handle when you are blocking down a spar.

This is the biggest real difference. The 372XP uses a conventional carburetor that you adjust with high and low speed screws. That works well and is easy to understand, but the saw runs best when someone tunes it for the fuel, altitude and temperature of the day, and many newer saws ship with limiter caps that restrict the range of adjustment.

The 572XP uses AutoTune, which senses running conditions and adjusts the fuel mixture on its own. That keeps the saw running consistently as you move from morning cold to afternoon heat, change fuel, or swap from a short to a long bar. For crews where several people share saws, AutoTune removes a lot of guesswork.

The trade-off is that AutoTune saws rely on electronics and are usually diagnosed with dealer tools when something goes wrong. Many old-school saw hands prefer the 372XP for that reason. Either way, run fresh fuel at the ratio in the operator's manual and keep the air filter clean.

The two saws are close in weight, and both are rear-handle saws meant for ground work, not climbing. The 572XP has a more modern layout with easy access to the air filter and spark plug, and its vibration damping is designed to be easy on your hands over a long day.

The 372XP's handling is familiar to anyone who learned on older Husqvarnas, and plenty of climbers still lower one on a line for big wood in the tree. If you do that, follow your crew's procedures, and remember that rear-handle saws should be run with two hands on the handles every time.

For ground work, think about how the saw balances with the bar you plan to run most. A 70cc saw with a 20-inch bar feels nimble for limbing and bucking, while the same saw with a 28-inch bar is front-heavy and better suited to felling and big rounds. Many crews keep two bars for one powerhead and swap based on the job. Whatever you run, check that the bar and chain combination is approved in the operator's manual, and keep the chain brake, chain catcher and throttle lockout in working order.

The 372XP has been around for a long time, so parts, bars, chain and know-how are easy to find. It is a saw a lot of people service themselves. The 572XP is newer, and its routine maintenance is just as simple: air filter, spark plug, fuel filter, bar and chain. More advanced troubleshooting may need a dealer.

Both saws need the same basics to last: clean air filter, sharp chain, correct fuel mix, a flipped and dressed bar, and a fresh spark plug when the old one is worn. Check the operator's manual for the correct plug and gap for your exact model, and see our chainsaw spark plug guide for how to read a plug.

Buying used is common in this size class, especially for the 372XP. Look for good compression, a clean cylinder if you can see the exhaust port, a smooth idle, a chain brake that stops the chain crisply, and no air leaks. Ask how it has been fueled and stored. A cheap saw that needs a top end is not a bargain.
list: Clean or replace the air filter often, especially in dusty or dry conditions
Sharpen chain before it starts making dust instead of chips
Flip the bar and dress the rails regularly
Use fresh fuel at the ratio in the manual
Replace the spark plug and fuel filter on a regular schedule

p: Pick the 572XP if you want the newer platform, AutoTune consistency, slightly more power and a saw that several people can share without retuning. It is the better fit for crews that run longer bars or cut hard wood all day, and for buyers who want a saw that will be supported for years.
Pick the 372XP if you find one available, know how to tune a carburetor, and value a simple saw with a huge parts and knowledge base. It remains a great removal and bucking saw.

Whichever you choose, wear chainsaw protective pants or chaps, a helmet with eye and hearing protection, gloves and boots, and get proper felling and chainsaw training. Our chainsaws section has more saw options if neither fits your work.

One more point for crews: standardizing matters. If the rest of your saws are newer AutoTune models, the 572XP fits your parts bin, fuel habits and service routine. If your shop is full of older carbureted Husqvarnas and a mechanic who tunes them by ear, a 372XP slots right in. Think about the bars and chain you already stock too, since matching sprocket, pitch and gauge across saws saves money and confusion on the truck.

faq.q: Is the 572XP better than the 372XP?
faq.a: The 572XP is newer, has AutoTune and is rated for a bit more power. The 372XP is simpler and easy to work on. For most removal crews the 572XP is the more modern choice, but both are strong 70cc saws.

faq.q: What bar length suits a 372XP or 572XP?
faq.a: Both commonly run bars from about 18 to 28 inches. Check the operator's manual for the bar and chain combinations approved for your model.

faq.q: Can I adjust the carburetor on a 572XP?
faq.a: The 572XP uses AutoTune, which manages the fuel mixture automatically. It does not need manual high and low speed tuning the way the 372XP does.

faq.q: Is the 372XP still available?
faq.a: It depends on the market. Emissions rules have limited sales in some areas, so availability varies.

title: Silky Saw Comparison: Sugoi, Zubat, Gomtaro & More
h1: Silky Saw Comparison: Which Silky to Carry
meta: Silky saw comparison for arborists: Sugoi vs Gunfighter vs Zubat vs Gomtaro vs Pocketboy. Blade shape, length and teeth, and which suits your work best.
dek: Five popular Silky saws, what each one is best at, and how to pick the right one for your saddle.

sections.h: Why a Silky saw comparison matters
p: Silky makes dozens of saws, and the names do not tell you much. This Silky saw comparison focuses on the five models tree workers ask about most: the Sugoi, Gunfighter, Zubat, Gomtaro and Pocketboy. All use Silky's hard, sharp, pull-stroke blades, and all cut fast. The differences are in blade shape, length, handle and how you carry them.

Before you pick a model, think about what you cut most. A pruning climber making finish cuts on live trees needs something different from a removal climber blocking down limbs, and a ground worker clearing brush needs something different again. Browse all the options in our hand saws and scabbards section.

All five are pull-stroke saws. That means the teeth cut as you draw the saw toward you, which keeps the thin blade in tension and lets it cut quickly with little effort. It also means you should let the saw do the work on the pull and use a light return stroke. Forcing the push stroke is the fastest way to bend or kink a hard Japanese blade.

Curved blades, like the Zubat, Sugoi and Gunfighter, pull into the wood as you cut. That makes them fast and efficient on overhead cuts and limbs at awkward angles, which is why most climbers carry a curved saw. The curve also helps the saw stay in the kerf when you are working one-handed.

Straight blades, like the Gomtaro, give more control on precise cuts and work well near the ground, on roots and on cuts where you want a flat, even face. Many arborists carry a curved saw on the saddle and keep a straight saw in the truck or on the ground.

Blade shape also changes how the saw feels when you start a cut. Curved blades bite quickly on the first pull, which is great overhead but can grab if you are not ready for it. Straight blades start more gently and track more predictably along a line, which helps when you want a precise undercut or a clean final cut close to the branch collar.

sections.h: Silky Zubat: the all-round climbing saw
p: The Zubat is the saw most people think of when they hear Silky. It has a curved blade, a comfortable rubber-covered handle and a scabbard that clips to your saddle. Sizes include 270, 300 and 330 mm, with the 330 mm size a favorite for climbers who want reach without excessive weight.
It handles most pruning cuts, deadwood removal and small limb work. If you only own one hand saw for climbing, the Zubat is a safe pick. See our Silky Zubat 13-inch page for details.

sections.h: Silky Sugoi: big wood without a chainsaw
p: The Sugoi is a large curved saw with an aggressive tooth pattern built for fast cutting in bigger wood. It comes in long sizes such as 360 and 420 mm and is heavier than the Zubat, so it suits climbers who want to handle bigger limbs without starting a top-handle saw.

It is a great tool for removal climbers working in tight spots and for crews working near structures or in noise-sensitive areas. The trade-off is weight on your saddle and a rougher cut than finer-toothed saws. Replacement blades are available, which helps when the blade dulls. Details are on our Silky Sugoi page.

The Gunfighter is a curved saw with a handle shaped for a secure, comfortable grip. Climbers who like it say it feels steady on overhead cuts and long sessions of pruning, and some find it easier to control one-handed.

It sits between the Zubat and Sugoi for many users: a solid all-round saw with a different feel in the hand. If you have tried a Zubat and found it tiring on your wrist, the Gunfighter is worth a look.

The Gomtaro is a straight saw with a rubber handle, available in many lengths and tooth sizes. Fine teeth leave clean finish cuts, while larger teeth cut faster in green wood. It is a strong ground saw, a good choice for root cutting, and a precise option for climbers who prefer a straight blade.

The Pocketboy is a small folding saw that fits in a pocket or a saddle pouch. It is a handy backup, useful for small cuts, and a favorite for groundworkers who need a saw now and then. It is not built for heavy limb work.
list: Zubat: curved, all-round climbing saw
Sugoi: large curved saw for bigger limbs
Gunfighter: curved, with a grip-focused handle
Gomtaro: straight blade for control, roots and ground work
Pocketboy: compact folding backup saw

sections.h: Tooth size, blade length and scabbards
p: Within each model, Silky offers different tooth sizes. Larger teeth remove wood faster in green limbs but leave a rougher face. Finer teeth cut slower but leave a cleaner finish cut, which matters when you are making pruning cuts that the tree has to close over. Most climbers working on live trees do well with medium teeth on a curved saw.

Blade length is a balance between reach and weight. A longer blade cuts bigger wood in fewer strokes and lets you reach a little farther, but it hangs heavier on your saddle and is harder to control in tight crotches. Climbers who do a lot of fine pruning often settle on a 270 to 330 mm saw, while removal climbers lean longer.

Scabbard design matters more than people think. A good scabbard lets you holster the saw one-handed, holds it securely when you are moving through the canopy, and clips firmly to your saddle. Many arborists also add a short tether so a dropped saw stays on the saddle instead of falling toward the ground crew.

sections.h: How to choose and care for your Silky
p: Match the saw to your main work. Pruning climbers usually start with a Zubat or Gunfighter. Removal climbers who want to avoid running a chainsaw on small limbs often add a Sugoi. Ground crews do well with a Gomtaro or Pocketboy.

Silky blades are hard and are generally replaced rather than resharpened in the field. Clean sap off the blade, keep it in its scabbard, attach it to your saddle with a lanyard when climbing, and keep your free hand clear of the cutting path. A sharp saw is safer because it takes less force.

Budget for replacement blades as part of the cost of ownership. Working climbers who prune every day can dull a blade in weeks, especially in gritty or dead wood. Keeping a spare blade in the truck means you are never stuck finishing a job with a saw that tears instead of cuts.

faq.q: Which Silky saw is best for tree climbing?
faq.a: The Zubat is the most common all-round climbing saw. The Gunfighter is a good alternative if you want a different grip, and the Sugoi is worth adding for bigger limbs.

faq.q: Can I sharpen a Silky saw?
faq.a: Silky blades are hard and are usually replaced rather than sharpened. Replacement blades are available for many models.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Sugoi and the Zubat?
faq.a: The Sugoi is larger, heavier and more aggressive for bigger wood. The Zubat is lighter and suits most pruning and smaller limb work.

title: How to Choose Arborist Rope for Climbing
meta: How to choose arborist rope for climbing: static vs low-stretch, 16 vs 24 strand, diameter and hardware fit, spliced eyes, and when to retire a line.
dek: A practical guide to picking a climbing line that works with your hitch or device and lasts.

p: Arborist rope is built for the specific demands of tree climbing: running over bark and friction savers, gripping friction hitches and devices, and holding up to sap, grit and daily abrasion. A climbing line is life-support equipment, so it must be approved for climbing by its manufacturer and meet the strength requirements in ANSI Z133.

There is no single best rope. The right arborist rope depends on whether you climb on a moving rope system or a stationary rope system, which hitch or device you use, and how you like a rope to handle. This guide covers the decisions in order. You can browse by type in our climbing rope section.

Arborist climbing lines are low-stretch or static. That is different from the dynamic ropes rock climbers use. Low-stretch lines give a little when loaded, which some climbers find comfortable on a moving rope system. Static lines stretch less, which makes ascending more efficient on a single rope because less of each step goes into stretching the rope.

Many SRS climbers prefer a firm static line, while many MRS climbers like a rope with a bit more give and a cover that holds a hitch well. Either way, a climbing line is not designed to catch a fall the way a dynamic rope is, so avoid any slack that could let you drop onto your system.

If you are just starting out, a lot of climbers recommend learning on a classic 16-strand line with a friction hitch. It teaches you how a hitch grabs and releases, it is forgiving of small mistakes in tending, and it wears well. Many climbers later add a firm static line for SRS once they move to mechanical devices.

sections.h: 16 strand vs 24 strand and other constructions
p: 16-strand ropes have a cover of 16 thick strands over a core. They are durable, forgiving with friction hitches and a classic choice for moving rope climbing. Their cover texture can be less smooth in some mechanical devices.

24-strand ropes use more, finer strands, giving a smoother, rounder rope that tends to run well in mechanical devices and gives smooth hitch performance. Kernmantle static ropes have a tight cover over a load-bearing core and are common for SRS. You will also see 12-strand and double-braid lines, mostly used for rigging. Learn more in 16-strand and 24-strand climbing rope.
list: 16 strand: durable, hitch-friendly, a classic MRS choice
24 strand: smooth, round, often device-friendly
Kernmantle static: firm, low stretch, common for SRS
Double braid: mainly for rigging, not climbing

p: Diameter is where many climbers get into trouble. Most arborist climbing lines fall between about 11 mm and 13 mm. Every mechanical device, rope wrench, pulley and friction hitch has a range of rope diameters and constructions it works with, and the manufacturer lists them. A rope that is too thin can slip; a rope that is too fat can bind and be hard to tend.

Also note that two ropes with the same listed diameter can feel very different because of cover firmness and construction. Before you buy, read the instructions for your device and check the rope maker's compatibility notes. When in doubt, test the combination low to the ground with a qualified person before you climb on it.
Hitch cord matters too: it should be a smaller diameter than your climbing line and made from a material that handles the heat of descending. Ask the cord maker which climbing lines it pairs with.

A 150-foot rope covers most residential trees when climbing doubled. Single-rope climbers can often use a shorter line for the same tree, but many still buy 150 or 200 feet for flexibility. Longer ropes cost more and weigh more in the bag.

Bright colors and patterns make a rope easier to see against foliage and easier to tell apart from rigging lines on the ground. A sewn or spliced eye on one end saves tying a termination knot, keeps the end compact and lets it pass through some hardware more easily. Splices should be done by a qualified splicer and follow the rope maker's procedure.

Buy a little more rope than you think you need. A line that is just long enough leaves no room to cut out a damaged section, to work a wider spread or to reach the ground from a high tie-in. Make sure there is always a stopper knot or other means to keep the tail from passing through your system, and that your rope is long enough to reach the ground from the highest point you plan to tie in.

sections.h: Matching rope to MRS and SRS
p: On a moving rope system, the rope runs over a branch union or through a friction saver, and you advance a hitch or device as you climb. The rope sees a lot of movement and heat at your hitch, so a durable cover and good hitch grip are priorities. Many MRS climbers like a slightly softer rope that their hitch bites into consistently.

On a stationary rope system, the rope is anchored and does not move over the tie-in point. You ascend with mechanical ascenders and descend with a device, so low stretch and consistent diameter matter most. A firmer static or kernmantle rope tends to give efficient ascents and predictable descents in SRS devices.

Many climbers end up owning both: a 16-strand line for MRS work and a static line for SRS access and work. If you can only buy one, choose based on the system you will use most and the device you will use with it. Our static climbing rope section covers popular SRS lines.

Inspect your climbing line before every climb by running it through your hands. Look and feel for cuts, glazing, flat spots, lumps, core damage, chemical contamination and excessive fuzzing. Keep the rope in a bag, away from saws, fuel and sun when not in use, and wash it according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Retire a rope that has been cut, shows core damage, has been shock-loaded or contaminated, or has reached the end of its service life per the manufacturer. Never use a retired climbing line for rigging; cut it up so it cannot go back into service by mistake. See rope care and splicing for accessories.

Keep a simple rope log with the purchase date, first use and any notable events such as a hard shock load or contact with a saw. It makes retirement decisions easier and helps crews track which line is which when several look alike.

faq.q: What diameter arborist rope should I buy?
faq.a: Most climbing lines are between about 11 mm and 13 mm. Pick the diameter your hitch, device and hardware are designed for, as listed by their manufacturers.

faq.q: Is 16 strand or 24 strand rope better?
faq.a: Neither is better for everyone. 16 strand is durable and hitch-friendly for moving rope climbing, while 24 strand is smoother and often works well with mechanical devices.

faq.q: Can I use rigging rope for climbing?
faq.a: No. Only use rope that the manufacturer has approved for climbing and that meets ANSI Z133 requirements as your climbing line.

faq.q: How long does arborist rope last?
faq.a: It depends on use, care and the manufacturer's guidance. Retire any rope that is cut, damaged, shock-loaded or contaminated.

title: Chainsaw Chaps vs Chainsaw Pants: Which to Wear
meta: Chainsaw chaps vs chainsaw pants for tree work: how protection works, comfort, climbing and ground use, standards and cost. Pick the right leg protection.
dek: How each option protects you, where each makes sense, and how to choose leg protection you will actually wear.

sections.h: How chainsaw chaps and pants protect you
p: Chainsaw chaps and chainsaw pants work the same way. Layers of long, strong fibers sit under the outer fabric. When a moving chain cuts through the outer shell, those fibers pull out and wrap around the sprocket, clogging the drive and stopping the chain or slowing it down sharply. That is why a cut garment must be retired: the fibers that protected you once are gone.

Neither option makes you cut-proof. Protection depends on chain speed, saw power and how the contact happens. Leg protection is a last line of defense behind training, good technique and a well-maintained saw with a working chain brake.

Protective fibers also only work where they are. Chaps and most chainsaw pants protect the front of the legs, because that is where most leg contact happens when you are standing and running a saw. Some styles extend protection around the calf or cover more of the leg. Match the coverage to how you work, and keep the saw away from the parts of your body that are not covered.

Chaps strap over your regular work pants, with protection on the front of the legs. They go on and off quickly, so ground workers can wear them when running a saw and take them off for chipper work, raking or climbing. They are usually the more affordable option and a single pair can fit several people.

The downsides are heat and fit. Chaps can be hot in summer, can shift around if not adjusted well, and often leave the backs of the calves uncovered. Many have a wrap-around lower section that adds calf protection. Browse chainsaw chaps for apron and full-wrap styles.

Fit chaps so the protective panel covers the front of your leg from the upper thigh to below the top of your boot, and snug the straps so the chaps do not slide around when you walk. Too long and they catch on brush and your boots; too short and they leave a gap above the boot where contact is common. Adjust them with the work pants and boots you actually wear.
list: Quick on and off
Usually less expensive
Can be shared across a crew
Can be hot and shift during work

p: Chainsaw pants build the protective layers into the trouser itself. Because they fit like regular pants, they move with you better when climbing, kneeling or walking through brush, and they do not shift. Many have venting, stretch panels and reinforced knees. Climbers who run saws in the tree often prefer them.

Chainsaw pants cost more, you need the right size, and you wear them all day whether or not you are cutting. Lighter, cooler designs from brands like Clogger and Arbortec have made all-day wear much more comfortable. See our chainsaw pants section.

Sizing matters more with pants than with chaps. Protective layers should cover your legs from the thigh to the top of your boot when you are standing, kneeling and crouching. Try them on with your boots and harness if you plan to climb in them, and look for a waist that stays put with suspenders or a belt. Suspenders are common on chainsaw pants because the protective layers add weight.

sections.h: Standards and labels to look for
p: In the US, chainsaw leg protection is commonly tested to ASTM F1897, and some products carry UL certification. European products are often rated to EN ISO 11393, which uses protection classes based on chain speed and design types that describe how much of the leg is covered. Read the label carefully and match what your employer requires.

ANSI Z133 covers leg protection for chainsaw operators in tree work. Requirements can differ between ground work and work aloft, so check the current standard and your company's policy rather than relying on habit or what the last crew did.

sections.h: Which to choose for your work
p: If you are a groundworker who runs a saw for part of the day and does a lot of other tasks, chainsaw chaps are a practical, affordable choice. Keep them on the truck and put them on every time you pick up a saw.

If you run a saw for much of the day, climb with a saw, or work in hot weather, chainsaw pants are often worth the extra cost because you will wear them consistently. Many professionals own both: chaps for occasional ground use and pants for days with heavy saw work.
The best leg protection is the one you actually wear. Choose a fit and weight that is comfortable enough for your whole shift.

Think about season and job mix too. Many crews keep a pair of lighter chainsaw pants for summer and heavier pants or chaps for cold-weather work. In wet conditions, look for water-resistant outer fabric so the protective layer does not get heavy and soaked. If you work brush-heavy sites, reinforced fronts and gaiters around the boot help pants last.

A pair of chainsaw chaps is usually the cheaper upfront purchase, and a set or two can serve a whole crew. Chainsaw pants cost more and are personal items, so each worker needs their own. Over a season, though, value comes down to wear. A protective garment that sits in the truck because it is hot or awkward protects nobody.

Look at durability features if you work hard on your gear: reinforced knees, abrasion-resistant panels at the boot, and stitching that holds up to climbing and brush. Protective layers can also be degraded by fuel, bar oil and solvents, so regular washing per the label and proper storage help both chaps and pants last.

Whatever you choose, budget to replace it. Protective gear that has been cut, is badly worn, or has reached the end of the maker's recommended service life should be retired. Our chaps and protective gear section covers both options in one place.

Inspect chaps and pants before each use for cuts, tears and worn areas. Wash according to the maker's instructions, since harsh chemicals or the wrong cleaning method can damage the protective fibers. Avoid patching cut areas: once the protective layer has been cut, the garment should be replaced.

Store protective gear away from fuel and solvents, and keep it out of direct sun when not in use. Pair leg protection with the rest of your PPE: helmet, eye and face protection, hearing protection, gloves and boots suited to saw work.

faq.q: Are chainsaw pants safer than chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: Both can provide similar protection when rated to the same standard. Pants stay in place and are often worn more consistently, which is a real safety advantage.

faq.q: Can you wash chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: Yes, but follow the manufacturer's instructions. The wrong cleaning method or harsh chemicals can damage the protective fibers.

faq.q: Do I need to replace chaps after a cut?
faq.a: Yes. Once the protective fibers have been cut, that area no longer protects you, so retire the garment.

faq.q: Do climbers wear chainsaw chaps in the tree?
faq.a: Many climbers prefer chainsaw pants because chaps can be bulky aloft. Check ANSI Z133 and your employer's policy for the leg protection required for your work.

title: NGK CMR6H vs BPMR7A: Chainsaw Spark Plug Guide
h1: NGK CMR6H vs BPMR7A: Chainsaw Spark Plug Guide
meta: NGK CMR6H vs BPMR7A explained: what the codes mean, which Husqvarna saws use which plug, setting the gap and reading plug color to diagnose your saw.
dek: Two common chainsaw plugs that look alike on paper but are not interchangeable, plus how to gap and read them.

sections.h: NGK CMR6H vs BPMR7A: the short answer
p: The NGK CMR6H vs BPMR7A question comes up because both plugs show up in Husqvarna and other professional saws. They are not interchangeable. The BPMR7A has a 14 mm thread and the CMR6H has a smaller 10 mm thread, so a plug that fits one saw will not even thread into a saw built for the other.

The right plug for your saw is the one listed in its operator's manual. This guide explains what the codes mean, which saws commonly use which plug, how to check the gap, and how to read an old plug to see how your saw is running. Both plugs are in our power equipment parts section.
NGK plug codes describe the plug's physical size and design. The letters and numbers are not random, and they explain why similar-looking plugs are not swappable.
list: BPMR7A: B means a 14 mm thread, P a projected insulator, M a compact design, R a resistor, 7 the heat range and A a special design feature
CMR6H: C means a 10 mm thread, M a compact design, R a resistor, 6 the heat range and H the thread reach
In NGK's system a higher heat range number means a colder plug, so a 7 is colder than a 6
The thread size difference alone means the two plugs cannot replace each other

sections.h: Which Husqvarna saws use which plug
p: The BPMR7A is a long-standing plug for many larger Husqvarna saws. The 372XP is a well-known example: Husqvarna lists the NGK BPMR7A, or an equivalent, for it. Many other older and larger Husqvarna saws use the same plug, which is why it is a common item to keep in the truck. See our NGK BPMR7A page.

The CMR6H is a compact plug with a smaller thread, used on many newer and smaller engines, including a number of handheld power tools and some top-handle and compact saws. Our NGK CMR6H page has more detail.

Saw models change over time, and plug specs can differ between versions and markets. Always confirm the exact plug for your saw in the operator's manual, on the manufacturer's parts lookup, or with an NGK cross-reference before you buy. If the plug in your saw now does not match the manual, the previous owner may have installed the wrong one.

A quick way to check on a saw you already own is to pull the existing plug and read the code printed on the insulator. That tells you what is installed, but not necessarily what belongs there. Compare it with the manual before ordering a replacement, and keep a note of the correct plug in your saw kit so the next person does not have to look it up.

The gap is the space between the center and ground electrodes. Too small and the spark is weak; too large and the saw can misfire, especially at high RPM. Husqvarna commonly lists a gap of 0.5 mm (0.020 in) for many of its saws, but check the manual for your model rather than assuming.

Check the gap with a wire-style gap gauge, not a flat feeler that can give a false reading on worn electrodes. Adjust only the ground electrode by bending it gently, never the center electrode. Thread the plug in by hand first so you do not cross-thread the cylinder, then snug it to the torque in the manual.

Never assume a new plug comes gapped correctly for your saw. Plugs are sold for many engines, and the factory gap may not match your saw's spec. Checking takes a few seconds and avoids a hard-starting saw on the next job.
list: Let the saw cool before removing the plug
Clean around the plug before removal so grit does not fall into the cylinder
Use a wire gap gauge and adjust only the ground electrode
Start the plug by hand and tighten to the manual's torque spec

p: An old plug tells you a lot about how a saw is running. After a normal run, the insulator around the center electrode should be a light tan or light brown. That generally means the fuel mixture and heat range are about right.

A black, sooty or wet plug points to a rich mixture: too much fuel or oil, a clogged air filter, too much idling, or a carburetor that needs adjustment. A white or very light, blistered insulator can mean the saw is running lean and hot, which can damage the engine. Oily deposits can point to the wrong fuel ratio. Use plug color as a clue, then check the basics before turning screws.

Read the plug after a good working run, not after a cold start and a few seconds of idling, which almost always leaves it looking darker than normal. If you change anything, such as a new air filter or a fresh tank of correctly mixed fuel, run the saw under load for a while before you judge the plug again.
list: Tan or light brown: running normally
Black and dry, sooty: rich mixture or dirty air filter
Wet and oily: too much oil, flooding or a fuel ratio problem
White or blistered: lean and hot; check for air leaks and fuel delivery

p: Replace the plug when the electrodes are worn or rounded, the insulator is cracked, deposits will not clean off, or the saw is hard to start and other causes have been ruled out. Many saw users replace the plug at the start of each season or on a regular service schedule, along with the air and fuel filters.

A plug is inexpensive, so keep a spare of the right type in your saw kit. If a lean condition shows up on the plug, have the saw checked before running it hard. Lean running can score a piston quickly. When in doubt, take it to a qualified service shop.

Fouling is the most common plug problem on saws that idle a lot or run old fuel. A fouled plug may clean up and run for a while, but deposits often come back quickly. Replacing the plug and fixing the cause, such as a dirty air filter, old fuel or the wrong mix ratio, is the lasting fix. Store saws with fresh, stabilized fuel or run them dry for long storage, following the manual.

faq.q: Can I use a CMR6H instead of a BPMR7A?
faq.a: No. The BPMR7A has a 14 mm thread and the CMR6H has a 10 mm thread, so they do not fit the same engines. Use the plug listed in your saw's manual.

faq.q: What spark plug does the Husqvarna 372XP use?
faq.a: Husqvarna lists the NGK BPMR7A or an equivalent for the 372XP. Confirm in your operator's manual, since specs can vary by version.

faq.q: What is the spark plug gap on a Husqvarna chainsaw?
faq.a: Husqvarna commonly lists 0.5 mm (0.020 in) for many saws. Check the operator's manual for your exact model.

faq.q: What color should a chainsaw spark plug be?
faq.a: Light tan or light brown is normal. Black and sooty suggests a rich mixture, and white or blistered suggests a lean, hot condition.
